**The Ownership Clause After the Long Dispute**

The chapter's book-brief (41:41–45) ended with parties in "distressing doubt," and verse forty-six steps back from the dispute to the rule that settles every such dispute: deeds are owned — good to the doer's own selves, evil to their own loss. The translators' "their own" renders Arabic reflexives (*anfusahum*) whose emphasis the verse stacks: the benefit is theirs, for themselves, and the phrasing is the sūrah's closing argument against the two errors that quarrels generate — the belief that God profits from obedience, and the belief that punishment is personal to the punisher. The chapter's own economy has been saying this since its beginning (no one's labor is lost, the reward is a taste, the Fire is a home the residents built), and now the rule is stated flatly enough to be memorized by the slowest hearer in the assembly, which is the mark of a verse the sūrah treats as a final clause of settlement: whoever wins the argument about the Book wins nothing; whoever does good has already been paid.

**No Surplus to God, No Shortfall**

The clause's theology is the negative the chapter has been proving through forty-five verses: creation's worship adds nothing to the Lord's treasury and its rebellion nothing to His loss, so all accounting is for the creature. The Spider chapter puts it exactly in these terms — "Whoever does good, it is to their own benefit. And whoever does evil, it is to their own loss. Then to your Lord you will all be returned" (45:15) — and Jonah states the bare rule beneath it: "Indeed, Allah does not wrong people in the least, but it is people who wrong themselves" (10:44). The difference from this verse is the object of the closing: there "people," here "creation" (*khalq*), and the widening is not stylistic: the God addressed as Lord of the creation (41:9's *fāṭir* passage) is the God whose non-injustice covers every creature in the smoke-and-order universe the sūrah has described, not merely the covenant class. The verse thus closes the chapter's cosmology and its ethics with one clause each: the Lord of all the created does no wrong to any of it.

**"To Their Own Selves" — the Ledger Without a Third Party**

Readers of this verse in the chapter's own light should note that the sūrah's middle already staged the same doctrine in narrative form: the enemies' assumption that God would not hear the small talk (41:22) was punished as a mistake about accounts, not manners; the organs testifying against the owners (41:20) proved that the deed never leaves the doer's house; the skin's speech (41:21) was the same ownership drama in a single organ. Verse forty-six states, in the chapter's legal register, what the chapter had dramatized in court and in flesh: there is no third party to whom your good deed flows. The good "is for yourselves" and the evil "is against yourselves" with the dryness of a contract clause, and the dryness is the verse's rhetoric — after fifty verses of thunder, rain, testimony, and welcome, the settlement is the shortest possible sentence with no image in it, because images were what the dispute argued about, and the ownership of deeds is not figurative. The Book does not need the hearer to feel; it needs him to know whose ledger he is filling.

**The Verse Against Victimhood and Against Bargaining**

The double clause disciplines the two ways a religious audience can misread its own fate. If the believer's good is "for themselves," piety is not a favor done to God for which His Book can be dunned for payment — the bargaining spirit that the chapter mocked (41:24's fruitless endurance — "Even if they endure patiently, the Fire will always be their home" — and 39:10's world-priceless Hereafter) is answered here in plain grammar, reward already assigned to its owner. And if the evildoer's evil is "against themselves," the claim of persecution by the message loses its nerve: the loss the hearer risks is not the prophet's malice but their own material, and the sūrah's warnings are then not weapons but signage. The Quran's standing rule of moral physics closes the Cave's record-scene in the same words: "And your Lord will never wrong anyone" (18:49) — the readers quote that clause as this verse's gloss — and its function in the chapter is to leave the audience no court of appeal but God, and no defendant but themselves.

**"Never Unjust to ˹His˺ Creation" — the Name Doing Double Duty**

The final clause's negation is the strongest available in Arabic: *mā anta ʿalayhim bi-ẓallāmin* would be "you are not a tyrant over them"; the verse's *wa-mā rabbuka bi-ẓallāmin li-l-khalq* is a permanent attribute-negation — your Lord is not, at any time, of the class of the unjust toward creation. The possessive "your Lord" does the same work verse forty-three's "your Lord" did — the same Subject of consolation — and the sūrah ties the two together: the God who forgives and punishes (41:43's pair) is the God whose punishment is definitionally not injustice, because justice is what the ownership clause just guaranteed — each soul receiving its own. The note in the sources records the readers saying exactly this, that the verse removes every ground for the complaint that God punishes unfairly: He takes from none what was not theirs to keep and gives to none more than their own. The mercy-first structure of the chapter (names of compassion at its head, forgiveness named before punishment at 41:43) stands uncancelled: severity in this book is not the opposite of the first sentence's mercy but its legal complement.

**Why the Chapter's Ethics End Here**

The sūrah's practical teaching, from the best speech (41:33) to the refuge from pricking (41:36) to the weariless choir (41:38), has been aimed at conduct; verse forty-six is the balance sheet that makes all of it rational, and the chapter ends its ethics here in the way it began — a statement that the system has no arbitrariness in it. What follows (41:47–54) turns to the Hour's knowledge, the associates' disappearance, the human's temperament, and the final challenge of the signs, but the moral load-bearing wall is in place: a reader who accepts the ownership clause accepts everything else the chapter said about patience, honesty, and refuge, because each of those teachings is the clause applied to a situation. The verse also completes a ring: verse three of the sūrah told the knowing that the book was expounded for their benefit; verse forty-six tells everyone that benefit itself is theirs to take or lose. The Book's claim about its own usefulness and the human claim about their own fate meet in one word — *l-anfusihim* — to their own selves — and the sūrah's ethics, finished, hands the reader the pen.
verses.47:
> With Him ˹alone˺ is the knowledge of the Hour. No fruit comes out of its husk, nor does a female conceive or deliver without His knowledge. And ˹consider˺ the Day He will call to them, “Where are My ˹so-called˺ associate-gods?” They will cry, “We declare before you that none of us testifies to that ˹any longer˺.”

**The Hour's Date in a Locked Drawer**

The chapter's final sequence opens by removing the question Mecca actually kept asking — when is this promise? — with an answer no committee of chronologists can appeal: to Him alone belongs the knowledge of the Hour. Luqmān turns the same lock: "Indeed, Allah alone has the knowledge of the Hour. He sends down the rain, and knows what is in the wombs" (31:34) — rain, wombs, and the Hour in one breath, which is why botany and obstetrics belong in verses about eschatology — and the Parties chapter converts the sealed date into a summons: "That knowledge is only with Allah. You never know, perhaps the Hour is near" (33:63). The sequence of the sūrah's own verbs matters too: knowledge is *ʿindahu* — with Him — an idiom of possession, and the chapter's last word about timing is thus not "it is hidden" but "it is owned," which removes the date from the market where the deniers hoped to buy it or debunk it.

**Fruit in the Husk, the Child in the Womb**

The minute clause — no fruit coming out of its sheath, no female conceiving or delivering, except by His knowledge — is the sūrah's answer to the scale of what the Hour's knowledge implies. The commentators note the pair's art: the husk's opening and the birth-canal's delivery are both *emergence*, a thing arriving in time at a moment no observer can predict, and the verse places the Hour's moment in the same class of emergences as the seed-coat splitting — events whose timing belongs, in the creatures' experience, to nobody's foreknowledge. The Thunder chapter gives the omniscience its inventory: "Allah knows what every female bears and what increases and decreases in the wombs. And with Him everything is determined with precision" (13:8), and the Cattle chapter closes on leaves and seeds: "Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth" (6:59). The Hour's hour is thus not withheld because it is far away; it is withheld because nothing comes to birth in this universe except through that same knowledge, and the distance was always in the questioners, not in the timing (41:44's "faraway place").

**"Where Are My Associate-Gods?"**

The Day's question is one of the Quran's most theatrical: He calls out to them, where are My partners? — and the sūrah's audience had already heard this interrogative at 46:5's "who are those you invoked besides Him?" (the question that opens the next section of this very chapter's family). Its force here is procedural rather than emotional: the court does not ask whether the partners are real but produces them, as a prosecutor produces the exhibit the defense promised, and the silence after the question is the evidence. The phrasing "My associate-gods" (shurakāʾī, the translation's own compound) puts possession on the lips of the accused's own theology for the last time, and the chapter's long argument about partners — the creation sequence that made them unable to create (41:9's "they did not create anything," the same logic) — now arrives at its only possible endpoint: the day names the missing.

**The Last Witness Statement — Nobody Will Testify**

Their reply is the verse's masterpiece, and it is a sentence about testimony: "We declare before you that none of us testifies to that" — the associates, and their worshippers with them, formally withdrawing the evidence. The sūrah has run on witnesses since verse nineteen (the gathered enemies, 41:19), with the organs deposing (41:20) and the skin delivering the closing statement (41:21), and here the chain completes in the reverse direction: the last testimony the court takes is the witnesses' recantation — the gods testifying that they were never gods. The reply is strictly a juridical act, a witness-bearing they now deny ever having offered, and readers should note that the men do not say "we lied" but "none of us testifies" — the register of the courtroom, where the case for partners fails not for falsehood but for want of witnesses, the sūrah's most devastating sentence about the polytheists' entire religion: a claim that cannot find one soul to attest to it, on the day when every soul wants to.

**"The Day He Will Call" — Why the Hour's Knowledge Comes First**

The two halves of the verse are a single argument by structure, and the order is exact: first the knowledge that no creature holds (the Hour), then the summons that no creature can dodge (the calling), and between them the fruit and the birth — the universe of small, punctual arrivals. The implication is the chapter's closing syllogism: the same knowledge that registers each seed's opening is the register in which the Day's hour is entered, and the God who is asked "where?" will ask, which means the question has a date fixed in that same drawer. The chapter that began its sign-cycle with "you see the earth lifeless" (41:39) ends it with the only sign that ever counted: the emergence of the moment, seed-sized and world-sized, in the mind of the All-Knowing. The associates cannot supply it, the Husayn of fruit cannot anticipate it, and the sūrah has been saying since verse two that the book which names it is sent down from the one who does.

**The Verse's Standing in the Chapter's End**

Positioned after the ownership clause (41:46) — each soul its own ledger — verse forty-seven closes the ledger's bookkeeping question (who keeps it, when it is audited, and who testifies), and it answers the doubt the Moses-verse named (41:45): doubt is distressing precisely because the doubter wants the date and the witnesses, and this verse takes both out of circulation. The sūrah's psychology of denial can now be stated with the clarity it has earned: the Meccan objection was never really "is this true?" but "will it be on time, and who will stand for it?" — the two questions a sealed drawer and a recanted witness answer absolutely. What remains for the chapter, as the next verse shows, is the partners' own performance on that day: not their defense but their disappearance — but the verse that says it will say it itself.
verses.48:
> Whatever ˹idols˺ they used to invoke besides Allah will fail them. And they will realize that they will have no escape

**The Verb of Vanishing**

*Ḍalla ʿanhum* — rendered "will fail them" — is the root of going astray and being lost, the same verb the chapter will choose for the most astray of men (41:52's *aḍallu*), and here it is not the worshippers who are lost but the worshipped. The verse's choice is worth the philology: the idols do not die here, though the Book's plainest description of them was always physical — gods "who cannot create anything but are themselves created. Nor can they protect or benefit themselves" (25:3) — and they do not argue; they go astray from the scene, vanishing from the story at the moment the story needs them. The sūrah has already said everything it will ever say about partners in the negative — they create nothing, they profit nothing, and for the wrongdoers there is "neither a close friend nor intercessor to be heard" (40:18) — and this verb is the sum: failure is not the idols' defeat but their withdrawal from the story at the moment the story needs them. An invocation whose object closes its doors is the chapter's last word on prayer to the unreal.

**"They Used to Invoke" — The Grammar of Habit**

The Arabic puts the idols' whole career in the imperfect of repeated past, *mā kānū yadʿūna* — that which they had kept calling — and the sūrah's audiences hear it as a record of practice, not conviction. The older readers stress that the clause is the verse's real verdict: nothing in it says the men ever believed the stones could save; it says what they did, repeatedly, in the face of every contrary evidence their own lives offered — which is the definition of the religion this chapter has described from the start: not a false theory but a habit sustained against its own data — the private-half assumption, "Allah did not know much of what you used to do" (41:22), and the public noise-policy (41:26) its civic half. When the verse says the invoked will fail, it describes habit meeting its term; the verbs of "invoking" and "failing" differ only in tense, and the whole of idolatry in this sūrah is a present tense that does not know it is past.

**"They Will Find That They Had No Escape"**

The realization-clause closes the sūrah's long trial with its quietest verb: *wa-ʿarafū* — and they will know — followed by the discovery that there is *lā maḥīṣa lahum*, no place of retreat for them, the noun of escape reserved in this chapter for its final hour: the condemned find that their condition was never one with exits in it. The verb "they will know" (*ʿarafo*) matters more than it looks: this is the knowledge of recognition, the dawning that confirms what the proof-letters said and what the habit denied, the recognition the prisoners' late cry voices elsewhere in this Book (32:12's seeing and hearing), and the verse's own knowledge-theme since forty-seven (the Hour's drawer, the seed's sheath). No new information arrives on that Day; what arrives is the end of the ability not to know, and the chapter's audience — who were offered the same facts in recitation — hear in this clause the precise definition of what they are refusing: not belief, but the delay of this recognition.

**The Oath They Will Still Try**

The source preserves the Day's matching scene from the Cattle chapter, where the same men, facing the same question, attempt one last evidence-based plea: "Their only argument will be: 'By Allah, our Lord! We were never polytheists'" (6:23), and the Cattle chapter answers that plea with its own verdict on swearing: "See how they will lie about themselves and how those ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them!" (6:24), the very verb of 41:48's first clause in another chapter's sentence. The pairing with this sūrah's forty-eight is exact in its cruelty: the oath is an invocation of the true God to deny the false ones, which is itself the scene's proof that men always knew which god was which — the sworn denial arrives one verse after the partners' failure because the failure is what provokes it, and it fails in turn. The chapter had said the private half long ago — "Rather, you assumed that Allah did not know much of what you used to do" (41:22) — the men who thought nothing was noticed will, on that Day, think the noticed could be sworn away, and the sūrah treats that reflex as data about the human animal, not as an argument worth answering at the bar.

**Why the Verse Has No Threat in It**

Remarkably, forty-eight announces nothing; it states a condition. No fire is described, no punishment is prescribed — the sentence is a report: the invoked gone, the escape found not to exist — and the quiet is the chapter's closing argument about the Day's mechanics. The punishment of the polytheists, in this sūrah's final accounting, is not an infliction but an inventory of what their own religion always was, and the sūrah's earlier grammar taught the readers to hear it: the skin spoke what the body did (41:21), the home built brick by brick was the Fire (41:28), and here the escape that was never there is discovered by the simple act of checking. The absence of threat-language is thus the most terrible thing in the passage: the verdict has become a property of the condemned, not a sentiment of the judge, and a sūrah that ends its court this way has already said everything divine justice needed to say in it. The All-Wise, the Praiseworthy (41:42's seal) stands behind the report exactly as He stood behind the offer.

**The Verse at the Chapter's Last Seam**

Forty-eight is the chapter's final sentence about the partners, and its brevity — two clauses where the polemicists of Mecca wrote books against the sanctuary's gods — is the sūrah's answer to the genre: it does not refute the gods, it attends their bankruptcy. From here the chapter leaves the courtroom entirely and turns, in its closing movement, to the one remaining exhibit — the human being's temperament when prosperity and adversity pass over it (41:49) — because the sūrah's last argument is not with the idols but with the psychology that kept calling them: the same "man" who never tires of asking for good and despairs when touched by harm, a creature the next verse will portrait in two sentences. What the chapter has spent forty-seven verses proving about heaven's ledger, it now spends seven proving about the heart's, and the seam is perfect: the partners failed (41:48's two clauses) — now let the reader see what kind of creature chose them, which is where the sūrah's final address begins.
verses.49:
> One never tires of praying for good. And if touched with evil, they become desperate and hopeless

**"The Human" as a Genre**

The Arabic puts *al-insān* — the human being, with the article that takes the whole species as its object — in the first clause of the sūrah's final triptych, and the translators' "one" is the right humility before it. Some readers in the classical lists took the verse to mean the disbeliever (IJ, Ṭ), and it is true that the portrait fits the Meccan case; but the stronger reading is the general one the sources themselves keep reaching for — a reflection on the frailty of the human condition, in which people vacillate from hope to despair and back (R) — because a sūrah whose court has just dissolved with the recanting of all witnesses does not spend its last chapters on a single class of defendant. The genre-reading has a structural benefit: the hearer who recognizes the portrait is not identifying an enemy but receiving a diagnosis, and the sūrah has been doing diagnosis since its first "turning-away" verses. The man of 41:49 is the reader, and that is the verse's whole argumentative method.

**"Praying for Good" — Asking Without a Ceiling**

The good he never stops asking for is, in the old glosses, wealth, health, and their like (IJ, IK, Ṭ), and al-Rāzī adds the psychology the verb requires: no amount satiates him so that he stops asking for more — the prayer has no termination condition, and *lā yaṭʿamu* ("he does not sate") makes the asking not an act but a state. The Book gives the same portrait its two coordinates elsewhere: "Indeed, humankind was created impatient: distressed when touched with evil, and withholding when touched with good" (70:19–21), and "humans ˹swiftly˺ pray for evil as they pray for good. For humankind is ever hasty" (17:11) — the second verse's confession being the sūrah's own, that the direction of this tireless asking is unreliable: the same tongue that begs for wealth begs, in anger, for harm. Fuṣṭilat's clause is thus the plain face of a known condition: man as the species whose requests are infinite and whose wisdom about them is nil.

**"Touched with Evil" — The Theology of Contact**

*Massa* — touch — is the verse's small verb, and it is the chapter's own: the damned of ʿĀd were made to "taste a humiliating punishment" (41:16), the disbelievers will "taste" severe punishment (41:27), mercy will be "tasted" (41:50, next verse), and torment finally "tasted" (41:50's close). The sūrah's metaphysics of experience is contact: good and evil are not arguments but surfaces that meet the skin, and the verse before us names the human as whatever reacts wrongly when the meeting happens. To the touch of evil his response is *qanūṭ* — despairing — a superlative form whose root means to be cut off, the man severed from the expectation of good. The pairing the chapter insists on is that the same organ of reception runs both of his states: the hand that reaches for more and the hand that lets go of everything are one hand, which is why 41:49's two clauses are, in form, a single sentence about touch.

**Despair Is the Same Religion as Greed**

The verse's halves are not two personalities but one, and the sūrah's audience should have learned it from the chapter's anatomy of the ear and heart (41:5, 41:26): the tireless asker and the instant despairer are the same creature because both are governed by circumstance rather than conviction — "there are some who worship Allah on the verge ˹of faith˺: if they are blessed with something good, they are content with it; but if they are afflicted with a trial, they relapse ˹into disbelief˺, losing this world and the Hereafter" (22:11), the Pilgrim chapter's verdict on exactly this weather-vane piety. The chapter does not say here that the man disbelieves; it says that his prayer and his despair are one motion viewed from two ends. That is why the triptych that opens with this verse is thesological rather than doctrinal: the illness of 41:49–51 is not a wrong creed but a self that has never been in contact with anything but its own fortune.

**The Counter-Portrait Nineteen Verses Back**

Set the man of 41:49 next to "those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then stand firm" (41:30), and the sūrah's design becomes visible: the steadfast receive from the angels precisely the two words this man cannot hear — "do not fear, and do not grieve" — a prohibition addressed, in the classical reading, to exactly the twin maladies: fear for what is coming and grief for what is lost. The chapter has built its final section as a mirror of its consolation section: where the allies hear the angels descend and say "do not fear and do not grieve" (41:30), the generic human's organs here oscillate between asking and collapse. The verse is not introducing new material; it is reissuing the chapter's first division — the two classes — in psychological rather than judicial language, so that the reader understands the trial of 41:19–24 and the welcome of 41:30–32 as outcomes of the same question: what do you do when something touches you.

**Why the Chapter Turns to Psychology Last**

The sūrah has defended its book against noise (41:26), distortion (41:40), and denial (41:41), and defended its prophet (41:43) and its language (41:44); having done so, it spends its final paragraphs not on the Meccans' arguments but on the human's temperament, and the placement is the chapter's last word about method. Proof that reaches only the convinced will not reach Mecca; so the sūrah makes its final exhibits the reader's own inconstancy — asking without end, despairing at a touch, presuming upon mercy (41:50), turning away when given (41:51) — and then, as if to answer the despair it has just drawn, promises that signs will keep arriving in the horizons and in the self (41:53). The chapter's ending is thus a treatment, not a threat: it has diagnosed the species so precisely that the final call to certainty is addressed to a patient who recognizes his own chart. Whoever reads 41:49 and sees a description of himself has already been read by it.
verses.50:
> And if We let them taste a mercy from Us after being touched with adversity, they will certainly say, “This is what I deserve. I do not think the Hour will ˹ever˺ come. And if in fact I am returned to my Lord, the finest reward with Him will definitely be mine.” But We will surely inform the disbelievers of what they used to do. And We will certainly make them taste a harsh torment

**"This Is What I Deserve" — Entitlement as Theology**

The exclamation — *hādhihi lī*, "this is mine" — is one of the Quran's small catchwords for the religious instinct of ownership, and the sources read it precisely: the man feels the mercy is owed to him (IJ, IK, R) or that God is pleased with him and so rewarded him (Ṭ). Its most famous sibling is Qārun's — "I have been granted all this only because of ˹my˺ knowledge" (39:49) and in the Story chapter's version, "He replied, 'I have been granted all this because of some knowledge I have'" (28:78) — and both scenes are cited in this verse's own margin, because Fuṣṭilat's man completes the theft that Qārun began: he does not merely credit his own knowledge; he converts the gift into property and the property into a forecast of final success. The clause is a miniature of the whole chapter's indictment, since its opening exchange: the men who demanded the recitation be drowned had already assigned themselves the venue, the argument, and now, in this verse, the verdict.

**The Logic Stolen from Verse Forty-Six**

Two verses back the sūrah established that whoever does good has it *for their own selves* (41:46), a rule meant to teach ownership of consequences; verse fifty shows the same ownership grammar mutated into a claim against God — "the deed is mine, therefore the reward is mine, therefore the next reward is mine." The readers' psychology is exact: nothing in the man's sentence mentions God as giver except to make Him a confirmer; the mercy is "tasted" (the verse's own verb, in the chapter's contact-language since 41:16), and the taste is taken as a signature on his own file rather than a gift from another's hand. This is why the chapter placed the ownership clause right before the presumption: the Book's just ledger is the one instrument that can be forged, and verse fifty demonstrates the forgery in real time — a man quoting, in effect, a corrupted copy of 41:46.

**"I Do Not Think the Hour Will Ever Come"**

The middle confession ties his economics to his eschatology, and the Book knows the type at its full length: the owner of the two gardens says it verbatim in his — "I do not think ˹this˺ will ever perish, nor do I think the Hour will ˹ever˺ come. And if in fact I am returned to my Lord, I will definitely get a far better outcome than ˹all˺ this" (18:35–36) — which is Fuṣṭilat's verse in a longer dress, down to the conditional "if I am returned." The syntax of the doubt is the datum: the Hour is not denied on evidence but *discounted as inference from his own case* — prosperity, to this mind, is a proof that no audit is coming — and the cave chapter shows the same inference collapsing into the loss of both worlds. The Smoke chapter's residents put its end point on record: when told that Allah's promise is true, "you said ˹mockingly˺, 'We do not know what the Hour is! We think it is no more than speculation, and we are not convinced'" (45:32) — the Hour demoted to rumor by men who were enjoying their credit.

**The Conditional That Keeps a God He Does Not Expect**

"And if in fact I am returned to my Lord, the finest reward with Him will definitely be mine" — the verse's most revealing phrase is its *if*: the man cannot bring himself to close the door on the meeting, so he reopens it as a favorable appointment. He will not surrender God, only his accountability; the return is allowed precisely to be a promotion ("the finest reward with Him"), his worldly balance sheet simply carried into the next office. The sūrah has already diagnosed this bargaining instinct — the trade the lost made when they preferred guidance for blindness (41:23's scene, whose ledger 2:16 describes in the Book's standing idiom) — and here the trade is eschatological: a God who is kept on retainer as guarantor of one's merits. The commentators are blunt about the class this verse describes: not the atheist but the confident man, the one whose religion is his own success story, and the sūrah gives his sentence the whole of its second half because that is the species of denial it expects to outlive Mecca.

**The Answer: Notification and a Taste**

God's reply begins without argument — "We will inform the disbelievers of what they used to do" — and the readers rightly note the choice: presumption is answered not with rebuttal but with briefing, the notification-motif that runs across the Book's Judgment Day ("then He will inform you of what you used to do" is the Qur'an's standard close of a dispute). The informing is the refutation, because the man's claim was about facts to be revealed at an audit; the audit, not a debate, decides it. And the clause's tail completes the chapter's tactile symmetry: he tasted a mercy and claimed it — "We will make them taste a harsh torment" — the verb of touch returned to the toucher, and the sūrah's contact-theology (41:16, 27, 49) closes on it. Reward and revenge in the same medium is the verse's theology of the human being as the creature that can only be argued with by experience.

**The Worst of the Three Portraits**

The triptych — the tireless asker (49), the presuming receiver (50), the turning ingrate (51) — places its worst in the middle, and the ordering is the chapter's final teaching. The first man is weak; the third is faithless; the middle man is both, plus a theologian: he has built a God who ratifies his greed and an afterlife that pays his dividends, which is the one state the sūrah has no remedy for inside the portrait itself. That is why the chapter turns next not to argument with this man but to the horizon and the self (53), and to the Witness who is sufficient without anyone's theology (53's close): the presuming heart cannot be reached by evidence, because it has evidence already — its own prosperity — and the sūrah answers it by promising that signs will keep arriving in places the man does not own. The verse thus stands at the chapter's hinge in its own small way: everything after 41:50 is about the God who outlasts our claims on Him — but the sentence that opens that movement belongs to the next verse.
verses.51:
> When We show favour to someone, they turn away, acting arrogantly. And when touched with evil, they make endless prayers ˹for good˺

**The Double Retreat**

The first clause's Arabic gives the turning two verbs for the price of one — *tawallā* and *nafā bi-janbihi*, turn away and thrust his side aside — the posture of a man rolling his body away from a caller, and the translators' "turn away, acting arrogantly" keeps both motions: refusal of the favor's Giver and self-removal from the room of gratitude. The source-note supplies the engine in one line: human beings turn away and withdraw because they consider themselves beyond need, which is the verse the Prophet of this very sūrah was reciting when the chapter of the Clot had cried: "Most certainly, one exceeds all bounds, once they think they are self-sufficient" (96:6–7). Fuṣṭilat's triptych thus ends where the first-revealed words began: the same self-sufficiency that made the man transgress is what makes him thankless, and the sūrah's psychology closes on the oldest of its diagnoses.

**A Twin Verse in the Isra**

The Night Journey chapter hands this verse's identical twin: "When We grant people Our favours, they turn away, acting arrogantly. But when touched with evil, they lose all hope" (17:83) — the same two-touch structure, favor turning the man away, evil ending his hope, the same verb of touch the sūrah has used since 41:49. The parallel is worth citing for what it changes: there the object is "people" in the plural of history, here the generic singular again, and the second half in Fuṣṭilat replaces despair with *endless prayer* — which is the more damning variant, because the man does not stop praying; he only redirects prayer to circumstance. The reader who compares the twins sees the sūrah's precise point: the type is not the one who has no God in affliction but the one whose God exists only in affliction, and whose relief therefore requires an exit from the presence of the One he just addressed.

**"Endless Prayers" — and the Quarrel About Them**

The final noun — *ḍuʿāʾ ʿarīḍ* — spread the old readers across a genuine range. One group took *ʿarīḍ* as long in words and short in substance, the broad, shallow, importunate petition (IK); another read it plainly: the disbelievers truly do beseech, earnestly and lengthily, in their affliction (Q, Ṭs) — and the second party added the sūrah's own gloss of the type, that they acknowledge God only when touched with trial, never in ease (Q). The disagreement dissolves into the verse's design: either way the man's prayer is measured by its expiry date, and 41:51 exists to stamp it. "Endless" in the first reading means verbose; in the second it means persistent; in both, it means mortal — a prayer that ends when the trouble ends is not worship but negotiation, and the chapter that began with prayer for good that never tires (41:49) now shows the negotiation at its final stage, conducted as though the counterparty were the affliction rather than Allah.

**Who Does What — the Verse's Quiet Grammar Lesson**

Mark the distribution of verbs across the triptych's last line: favor is something *We* actively show ("When We show favor"), while evil is expressed in the passive of touch ("when touched"), and the older readers press the asymmetry into a rule of theology: "˹Say,˺ 'Whatever good befalls you is from Allah and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself'" (4:79), the Women chapter's sentence that assigns grammar its ethics. The man of 41:51 does exactly the opposite with the same data: he attributes favor to himself (41:50) and — the verse here completes the portrait — attributes God to the evil, addressing his petitions to the moment of contact while his moments of giving leave him unthanked. The sūrah's two-verb clause is thus a miniature reversal of 4:79's order of gratitude, and the chapter places it after its own ledger verse (41:46) so that ownership, entitlement, and ingratitude stand revealed as one fault in three costumes.

**The Amnesia That Completes the Portrait**

The Book's other long description of this man's prayer supplies what this verse leaves between its clauses: "Whenever someone is touched by hardship, they cry out to Us, whether lying on their side, sitting, or standing. But when We relieve their hardship, they return to their old ways as if they had never cried out to Us to remove any hardship" (10:12) — the three postures, the full liturgy of distress, then the clean forgetting, the past tense of his own pleading erased. The Yunus-verse explains the "when" of Fuṣṭilat's second touch: the endless prayers are endless only inside the affliction, and the verse's cruelty is that the man's relief requires the fiction that he never begged. The sūrah's triptych now has its complete subject — he who asks without satiation (49), claims what he receives (50), and un-says his own kneeling (51) — and the chapter's next movement can proceed on the assumption that this portrait, not argument, is what Mecca will remember of these verses.

**Why the Triptych Is Not the End**

Three verses of psychology with no verdict attached — that is the fact of 41:49–51, and it matters: the sūrah that has thunderbolted nations and emptied courts now simply describes, and the description is the sentence. The portrait is left open-ended because the chapter has one instrument left, the one that started it: the Reminder itself, which will be vindicated (52), evidenced in the horizons and the self (53), and closed over by the Witness (54). The man who prays only when touched is exactly the being for whom a book of signs — rather than a book of threats — is the merciful form of address, and the sūrah's final three verses are built to his diagnosis: argument cannot hold him, but what he sees will outlast his mood. What the chapter now asks its audience to imagine, before it shows them the signs, is the shape of a denial measured against the book's own origin — that question is the next verse's work, and this one has done its part by telling us what the questioner looks like when he stops asking.
verses.52:
> Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Imagine if this ˹Quran˺ is ˹truly˺ from Allah and you deny it: who can be more astray than those who have gone too far in opposition ˹to the truth˺?”

**The Last Command of the Long Debate**

The chapter's closing sequence has run from the Hour's sealed drawer (41:47) through the partners' disappearance (41:48) to three verses of human physiology (49–51); now, at the end of the argument, comes the third and last *qul* of this sūrah's final movement — Say: have you considered? (earlier commands of the same form opened the chapter's creed-paragraph with "I am only a man" in 41:6 and the twin announcement of the book's twin offices in 41:44). The imperative marks the transition the whole chapter has engineered: description gives way to address once more, and the address is not a threat but a question, the same mode in which the sūrah has posed every decisive challenge (41:33's "whose words are better?" and 41:40's "who is better?"). Five hundred verses of Qur'anic polemic have no stronger ending available than a question the audience must answer against itself, and Fuṣṭilat chooses exactly that.

**The Conditional That Removes the Book**

"Imagine if this is from Allah and you deny it" — the verse's thought-experiment performs, for the whole Quran, the same operation 41:44 performed for its Arabic: there the language was inverted to show the objection was never about language; here the source is inverted to show the denial was never about evidence. Suppose, the verse says, the premise you dispute is true — and see what your denial becomes: not a mistaken conclusion but a condition of soul, measurable without settling the question you came to settle. Rāzī, in the source's summary, reads the whole clause as the sūrah's answer to 41:5's declaration — "Our hearts are veiled against what you are calling us to, there is deafness in our ears, and there is a barrier between us and you. So do ˹whatever you want˺ and so shall we!"" — and the fit is exact: the veil-thesis claims that the disagreement is a matter of insulation, and the conditional replies that even granting their own fear of contact, the position they have taken is not insulation but perdition. The objection of 41:5 is given one last hearing at 41:52, and dismissed by arithmetic rather than thunder.

**"Shiqāq" — the Rupture's Anatomy**

The noun the verse ends on, *shiṭāq*, the translation's "opposition (to the truth)," is from the root of cleaving and splitting — the word a rope gets when it parts — and it enters the Quranic vocabulary already freighted with the sense of schism, faction, and defiance (the same noun governs the parting of the People of the Book after the clear proofs came to them in the Cow's warning, and the split of every faction that has turned a community into camps). The source-note defines its force here: fracture joined with defiance, the deniers "far from Allah in both conduct and character." The chapter has spent fifty-one verses describing distances of the heart — veils, coverings, deafness, the faraway place (41:44) — and 41:52 names the limit of that geography with a word about tearing: this is not a wall anymore; it is a severed bond, and a severed bond does not need to be argued, because it has already fallen away.

**"Who Is More Astray?" — the Superlative of Loss**

The interrogative is the sūrah's signature device in its negative form (41:33 asked "whose words are better?" and crowned a class; here the superlative asks "who is more astray?" and finds no one), and the parallel elsewhere sharpens it: "And who could be more astray than those who call upon others besides Allah—˹others˺ that cannot respond to them until the Day of Judgment, and are ˹even˺ unaware of their calls?" (46:5), the Sandhills chapter's version of the same ranking applied to idol-prayer. Fuṣṭilat's ranking is worse because its object is narrower: not a wrong act but a stance toward a specific book, "this" — *hādhā* — the present Quran in the hearers' hands, denied by men who had it before them for years, watched it grow, and could not produce its opposite. The chapter's final word on the Meccan condition is thus comparative rather than absolute: the denier of the Reminder is not declared a sinner at a distance; he is asked, in front of the record of the whole sūrah, to name anyone further gone than himself, and the question ends where an answer would have begun.

**The Twin in the Sandhills**

The Sandhills chapter preserves this verse's closer twin, and the sources print them together: "Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'Consider if this ˹Quran˺ is ˹truly˺ from Allah and you deny it, and a witness from the Children of Israel attests to it and then believes, whereas you act arrogantly'" (46:10), where the same conditional is settled on the spot by an insider witness and the charge becomes pride rather than doubt. The pairing shows the two registers of one argument — Fuṣṭilat leaves the verdict to the hearer's arithmetic, al-Aḥqāf names the evidence and the motive — and the humility of Fuṣṭilat's form is its point: a sūrah that has already presented its exhibits in full (cosmology, precedent, court, psychology) does not add testimony; it lets the shape of the denial convict without comment. The reader of both chapters should hear 46:10 as this verse's footnote, and 41:52 as the Sandhills' argument stripped to its bare conditional, which is also the form in which it outlives the courtroom.

**Why the Chapter Has One Verse Left to Prove**

Structurally, 41:52 is the sūrah's last word addressed to the opponents in the mode of dispute; what follows (41:53–54) is addressed about them, not to them — the promise of showing the signs, and the summing verdict of the Witness — and that order is the chapter's final epistemological statement. A question like this one ("who is more astray?") assumes an audience capable of answering, and after 41:49–51 the sūrah has described why most are not; the remaining two verses therefore switch to divine first person — *We will show them*, *We will inform them* (41:50's verb recurring) — and let history and creation do the convincing that argument left unfinished. This is why 41:52 sits where it does: it is the hinge that turns rhetoric in on itself, questions the questioners once, and then hands the case over to the witnesses every later reader can check. The next verse's promise begins the transfer; this one ends the trial by closing the defendant's brief instead of the judge's.

> We will show them Our signs in the universe and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that this ˹Quran˺ is the truth. Is it not enough that your Lord is a Witness over all things

**The Future Tense of Proof**

*Sanurīhim āyātinā* — We will keep showing them — the sūrah's most optimistic verb-form, a first-person plural imperfect with God as its subject and open-ended time as its adverb. The verse is famous in the Book's own reception precisely because it converts evidence from a present-tense demand into a divine promise: the signs are not waiting for human discovery; they are scheduled for demonstration, and the chapter that has spent its length exhibiting the already-visible ones (rain, earth, heaven, testimony, organs, skin) now commits the unseen future of the same exhibit-list. Many of the commentators understood the promise at its plainest: the sūrah is saying that the argument will not be left to the hearers' impatience; God answers the question "who can be more astray?" (41:52) by taking over the case-file of proof across history itself.

**The Two Witnesses, and What the First Readers Made of Them**

The horizons and the selves — *al-āfāq wa-l-anfus* — gathered a spectrum of referents that is itself instructive: the conquest of the lands around Mecca (R) or the regions to which Islam spread (IJ, Q, Ṭ); the taking of Mecca itself or the day of Badr as the sign "within" (Q, R, IJ); the destruction of other civilizations and the withholding of rain (Q, IJ); and the bodies' illnesses, the celestial bodies and the alternation of night and day, and the stages of human life from conception through birth to death (Q, R), in the same list the Pilgrim chapter gives when it turns the embryo into evidence (22:5's stages, cited in that chapter's own sign-catalogue). The verse's genius is that it licenses the whole spectrum at once: the promise is not "the next sign will be X" but "the showing will not stop until the seeing is total," and the plural of readers was wise enough to keep every candidate on the list rather than pick one. A verse with a closed referent proves one thing; this one proves by method.

**The Self as Second Laboratory**

That the inner witness is not a metaphor but the same kind of data as the outer is guaranteed by the Book's near-verbatim twin: "There are ˹countless˺ signs on earth for those with sure faith, as there are within yourselves. Can you not see?" (51:20–21), the Chapter that scatters the pair into the earth and the soul and closes with the smallest possible imperative, *see*. Fuṣṭilat adds what the scattering chapter lacks — the *until* — making sight a term of proof rather than an offer; and its own earlier verses have already filled the "selves" with forensic content: the organs as witnesses (41:20), the skin's confession (41:21), the ear's disease (41:44). The human being who cannot trust his own anatomy in the trial of 41:19–24 is the same being whose anatomy will now testify to the truth of the book, and the verse's ambition is exactly to close that circle: the courtroom and the laboratory are one body.

**The Inward School's Reading of the Pair**

The great esoteric readings — the chapter's own sources preserve them at length — saw in the two witnesses one witnessing: al-Wāsiṭī, an early master of this discipline, is reported saying that God is manifest in everything through that which He discloses of it, and that whoever examines the things found nothing other than Him; Ibn ʿArabī, who quotes this verse often, mapped the horizons onto everything outside the human and the selves onto the microcosm in which the cosmos' realities are gathered, concluding that when both affairs are understood together, "we come to know Him and it becomes clear that He is the Truth." Whatever weight a reader gives these readings, they are faithful extensions of the verse's own grammar: the promise is that the showing continues *until clarity*, and clarity, in the inward school's vocabulary, is the disappearance of the distinction between sign and signifier. The plain sense survives them; they make the plain sense large.

**"Until It Becomes Clear That It Is the Truth" — and the Pronoun's Freedom**

The purpose clause hangs on a bare pronoun — *annahu* — and the sources list its candidates without closing the list: the Quran (IJ, Q), the religion of Islam (Q), the whole message the Prophet carries (IJ), his true prophethood (Q), or — with the antecedent supplied as "everything" — the truth of all created things, or God Himself, so that it reads "that He is the Truth." The ambiguity is not a flaw the sūrah failed to repair but an economy it performed: the clause makes every fulfilled sign confirm every candidate, so that conquest, rain, embryology, and the self's own testimony each count as proof of the book and of its Sender at once. And the verb of clarity — *yatabayyana* — is of the same root the chapter has worn since its title (41:3's expounded verses, 41:52's veils removed), and here at last it names the end of that process: exposition (tafsīl) exists to produce clarity (bayān) by showing what the veil refused to see. The sūrah's final epistemological word is its first adjective completed.

**"Is It Not Enough That Your Lord Is Witness Over All Things?"**

The closing question gives the proof-theory of the verse its seal: *a-wa-lam yakfi bi-rabbika annahu ʿalā kulli shay'in shahīd* — and is it not sufficient that your Lord is over everything a witness — and the same formula stands on the lips of the Women chapter's parallel: "Allah is sufficient as a Witness" (4:79). A witness is needed when the parties dispute, and God's witnessing is the sūrah's answer to the structure of dispute: every sign He shows is already witnessed in the showing, so that the promised endless demonstration (first clause) and the sufficient Witness (last clause) are one claim twice — the truth will be made clear from outside and inside because it has never been un-witnessed. The verse thus converts the trial of the chapter's middle into an exhibit that proves itself; the courtroom did not adjourn — it was dissolved into observation. What the sūrah's final sentence now names is the one state that survives the dissolution: the doubting of the meeting itself, and the God who is greater than that — in the next verse's last words.

> They are truly in doubt of the meeting with their Lord! ˹But˺ He is indeed Fully Aware of everything

**Two "Indeed"s and a Closed Book**

The chapter's final sentence opens with *a-lā* — the particle of summons, "do you not see? / lo!" — a word that, in the Quran's register, is used to pull an inattentive assembly to its feet for what is being said about them, and it appears here twice, once before the disease and once before the cure. The effect of the doubled particle at the end of fifty-four verses is structural: the sūrah dismisses no one, narrates no final scene, threatens nothing new; it says, in effect, *look — this is where you stand*. Commentators have noted how few Makkan sūrahs close so quietly, and how this one's brevity answers its own opening: verses that began by calling the book a revelation from the Most Merciful (41:2) end by naming the human condition and God's total awareness of it, mercy's object and mercy's witness compressed into two clauses. The chapter that spent half its length expounding has, at the end, nothing left to expound: only the standing of the reader and the encompassing of his Lord.

**"The Meeting with Their Lord" — the Hour Named by Its Verb**

*Liqāʾ* — meeting — is the Hour's gentlest name, and the chapter has prepared it everywhere: the organs' testimony is the meeting's procedure, the angels' descent its courier service, and the skin's speech its transcript; elsewhere the Book names the same state's denial in one clean line: "Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, being pleased and content with this worldly life, and who are heedless of Our signs" (10:7), which is the sūrah's own diagnosis (41:49–51) filed under the meeting's heading. But the word's true echo is inside the chapter, forty-six verses back: the great command to repel evil with what is better closed with "none is *granted* this (*yulaqqā*) except those who are patient" (41:35), and the passive of *l-i-q-y* there — to be made to receive, to be met with a gift — is the same root as the meeting here. Fuṣṭilat's last word about the Hour therefore completes its last word about ethics: the meeting is what the patient were being fitted to receive, and doubt of it is not an intellectual position but a failure of the capacity to be met. The sūrah has said, in its final sentence, that everything it taught was about this.

**"He is Fully Aware of Everything" — the Encompassing as Attribute**

The closing phrase translates *muḥīṭ* — encompassing, encircling, the participle of the root used for a wall that surrounds a garden and for water that closes on a ship — and the sources record the small, consequential argument over what He encompasses us *with*: most read the verse's final attribute as power and knowledge (IK, Q, R), while others press the Quran's own pairing of the verb's objects and conclude that only two attributes are ever said to encompass all things: the angels' prayer, "Our Lord! You encompass everything in ˹Your˺ mercy and knowledge" (40:7), and "Allah certainly encompasses all things in ˹His˺ knowledge" (65:12). Read as the second party reads it, the sūrah's last word rhymes with its first: the chapter that descended from the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful (41:2) closes on an encompassment in mercy and knowledge, and the doubt of the meeting — verse fifty-four's subject — is enclosed from both sides by what the doubler cannot escape and cannot outrun.

**The Enveloped, and the Face That Remains**

The commentators who read the encompassing inwardly push it one step further, and their step is worth the record: al-Kāshānī glosses that nothing escapes His encompassing because nothing has being, reality, or self apart from what His knowledge and His being give it — an argument the sources anchor in the Quran's own annihilation-verses: "Everything is bound to perish except He Himself" (28:88), and "Every being on earth is bound to perish. Only your Lord Himself, full of Majesty and Honour, will remain forever" (55:26–27). The reader should weigh this as the chapter's inner dimension, not as its last word — but it is a fitting last word to weigh, because a sūrah that has described a doubt (41:54's first clause) in a book (41:41–42), before a court (41:19–24), under a sky (41:9–12), arrives finally at the sentence that leaves nothing outside: the doubting, the book, the court, and the sky are all inside the encompassment, and only the Encompasser remains. The chapter's restraint in the end is its doctrine: it says awareness, not verdict, because at the end there is no verdict that is not already contained in it.

**How the Chapter Ends by Beginning Again**

Fuṣṭilat's structure now closes visibly: its first verses told the audience that the book was expounded for people who know (41:3) and that denial was a choice made after hearing (41:4–5); its last verses tell them that denial is a doubt about the meeting, and that the One they doubt is aware of everything — the ring is exact because the whole sūrah has been one long answer to the sentence "our hearts are veiled against what you are calling us to" (41:5). Between the ring's endpoints it has laid the whole apparatus: creation, precedent, court, ethics, consolation, signs, psychology, promise; at the endpoints it has only the condition and the encompassing awareness of it, which is what a reader is left with when expounding is finished. The chapter thus ends where teaching always ends for this book — not with argument concluded but with the hearer seen, and the seen thing given one more chance to see: which is why the final clause is an attribute of God, not a sentence about the audience — the sūrah's last act is to leave its verdict with the only Judge its own verses have been honest about.

**The Sūrah's Own Last Testimony**

One small fact belongs to the chapter's end: this is the final verse of a sūrah whose opening words the tradition made the criterion for whether the bow belongs in worship here (the sources recorded the dispute over 41:37–38 precisely as a question about the prostration in the recitation), and a community that recites these fifty-four verses weekly in the daily prayers repeats, at the end of every reading, that doubt of the meeting is real and that awareness is total — the chapter's argument re-enacted by every mouth that carries it. A text that ends on *muḥīṭ* has described its own position too: it is not the book that encloses its readers; it is the book recited inside an enclosure, and the last thing Fuṣṭilat ever says is that the enclosure is made of knowledge and mercy. Everything before that sentence is exposition; this is the sūrah, and the sūrah ends.
